final_proof:
The claim as written is false. There is also a typing issue for general \(V\): a series of vectors in \(V\) has a sum in \(V\), whereas \(r\) is declared only to be a positive real number. The following counterexample uses \(V=\mathbb R\), so the asserted conclusion is meaningful and the typing issue does not arise.

Fix any \(r>0\). Let \(I=J=K=\mathbb N_0\), and define \(v_0=r\) and \(v_i=0\) for every \(i\ne0\). Enumerate \(K\) by \(k_n=n\), and enumerate \(J\) by
\[
j_0=1,\qquad j_1=0,\qquad j_n=n \quad(n\ge2).
\]
Both displayed sequences are bijective enumerations of \(\mathbb N_0\), and the nonzero support \(\{i:v_i\ne0\}=\{0\}\) is contained in \(J\cap K\). Nevertheless,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}v_{j_n}=r,\qquad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}v_{k_n}=0.
\]
Indeed, the first series includes \(v_{j_1}=v_0=r\) and all its other terms vanish, while the second series omits \(v_{k_0}=v_0\) and all of its terms vanish. Both series are absolutely convergent, but only the first has sum \(r\). Hence the claimed equivalence is false.

The natural corrected statement is obtained by starting both series at \(n=0\) and by taking the proposed sum \(s\) to lie in \(V\): for every \(s\in V\),
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_{j_n}\text{ converges absolutely to }s
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_{k_n}\text{ converges absolutely to }s.
\]
We prove this corrected statement. Assume first that \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_{j_n}\) converges absolutely to \(s\). Write
\[
A_N=\sum_{n=0}^N v_{j_n},\qquad L=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lVert v_{j_n}\rVert<\infty.
\]
For every \(M\), each nonzero term among \(v_{k_0},\ldots,v_{k_M}\) has its index in the support of the family and therefore in \(J\). Since both enumerations are injective, these nonzero terms correspond to distinct terms of the \(J\)-series. Zero terms make no contribution, and hence
\[
\sum_{m=0}^M\lVert v_{k_m}\rVert\le L.
\]
These scalar partial sums are increasing and bounded, so \(\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\lVert v_{k_m}\rVert<\infty\). The vector partial sums are therefore Cauchy, and completeness of \(V\) implies that \(\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}v_{k_m}\) converges to some \(t\in V\).

We now prove \(t=s\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) such that
\[
\sum_{n>N}\lVert v_{j_n}\rVert<\varepsilon.
\]
There are only finitely many nonzero indices among \(j_0,\ldots,j_N\). Each is in \(K\), so there is an \(M\) such that all of them occur among \(k_0,\ldots,k_M\). For every \(P\ge M\), canceling these common terms shows that the difference between \(\sum_{m=0}^P v_{k_m}\) and \(A_N\) consists only of distinct terms whose positions in the \(J\)-enumeration are greater than \(N\). Thus the triangle inequality gives
\[
\left\lVert\sum_{m=0}^P v_{k_m}-A_N\right\rVert
\le \sum_{n>N}\lVert v_{j_n}\rVert<\varepsilon.
\]
Letting \(P\to\infty\) gives \(\lVert t-A_N\rVert\le\varepsilon\). Absolute convergence also gives
\[
\lVert s-A_N\rVert\le\sum_{n>N}\lVert v_{j_n}\rVert<\varepsilon.
\]
Consequently \(\lVert t-s\rVert<2\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary, \(t=s\). This proves one implication. Interchanging \(J\) and \(K\) proves the converse and completes the proof of the corrected statement.
